stem.text: Write the equation to represent the lattice energy, ΔHlatt, of calcium sulfide, CaS.

guidance: If reverse lattice energy equation is given CaS(s) → Ca<sup>2+</sup>(g) + S<sup>2–</sup>(g) award [1] if all species and state symbols are correct.

explanation.text: Lattice energy is the enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic solid is formed from its gaseous ions. So the equation starts from the separate gaseous ions, Ca<sup>2+</sup>(g) and S<sup>2–</sup>(g), and ends with one mole of the solid, CaS(s). M1 is for the right species (ions on the left, the compound on the right) and M2 is for the state symbols: (g) for both ions and (s) for the lattice.

reasoningChain: Recall the definition: gaseous ions → one mole of ionic solid.
Write the ions with their charges: Ca²⁺ and S²⁻, both (g).
Write the product as CaS(s) and check one mole is formed.

inferredMistakes.text: Writing the equation from the elements, Ca(s) + S(s) → CaS(s), which is the enthalpy change of formation rather than lattice energy.
Writing the reverse process, CaS(s) → Ca²⁺(g) + S²⁻(g), which the MS limits to [1].

stem.text: Explain why the value of ΔHlatt of CaS is negative.

guidance: I formation of the lattice / solid / CaS.
I reference to energy required to break bonds.
CON bond formed is clearly covalent, e.g. Ca–S.

points.text: (ionic) bonds are formed / the ions bond

explanation.text: Energy is always released when bonds form, so any process that only makes bonds is exothermic. In the lattice energy process nothing is broken: the separate gaseous ions are attracted to each other and ionic bonds form as the lattice builds, so ΔH<sub>latt</sub> is negative. The MS wants the cause (bonds form between the ions), which is why simply restating 'exothermic' or 'energy released' is ignored.

reasoningChain: Look at what happens in the lattice energy equation: gaseous ions come together into a solid.
Identify that ionic bonds are formed and none are broken.
Bond formation releases energy, so ΔH is negative.

inferredMistakes.text: Saying only that the process is exothermic or releases energy, which repeats the question instead of explaining it.
Stating that energy is needed to form the bonds, which contradicts the answer.

stem.text: State the order of the ΔHlatt values of CaS, MgO and KCl, from most negative to least negative.

points.text: M2 CaS (and MgO) the ions / particles are more highly charged than KCl or KCl has ions with the smallest charge ora
M3 MgO the ions/particles are smaller than CaS or MgO has the smallest ions ora

explanation.text: The size of a lattice energy depends on how strongly the ions attract: it becomes more negative when the ionic charges are larger and when the ions are smaller (closer together). MgO and CaS both contain 2+ and 2– ions, so they are far more negative than KCl, whose ions are only 1+ and 1–. Between the two 2+/2– compounds, Mg2+ and O2– are smaller than Ca2+ and S2–, so MgO is the most negative. The order is MgO > CaS > KCl.

The MS gives the charge comparison (M2) and the size comparison (M3) separately, and it ignores 'charge density' for both, so the answer has to talk about charge and size as two separate factors. It also accepts quoting all four charges for M2.

reasoningChain: Compare ionic charges: MgO and CaS are 2+/2–; KCl is 1+/1–, so KCl is least negative.
Compare ionic sizes for the two 2+/2– compounds: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ are smaller than Ca²⁺ and S²⁻.
Smaller ions are closer together and attract more strongly, so MgO is most negative.
State the order: MgO, CaS, KCl.

inferredMistakes.text: Using 'charge density' to explain both factors, which the MS ignores for M2 and M3.
Talking about atoms or nuclear charge instead of the charges and sizes of the ions.
Putting CaS above MgO by assuming that the heavier compound has the larger lattice energy.

stem.text: The enthalpy change of formation, ΔHf, of Cl–(g) or Mg2+(g) is the energy change when one mole of gaseous ions forms from the element in its standard state at 298 K.
enthalpy change of formation of chloride ions, Cl–(g) = –243 kJ mol–1
enthalpy change of formation of magnesium ions, Mg<sup>2+</sup>(g) = +2336 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>
The enthalpy change of formation of Cl–(g) can be calculated using two energy changes only.

guidance: If this is given in symbols we will accept ΔHat, ΔHatom or ΔHatomisation. If symbols and words are given, I the symbols.
If this is given in symbols we will accept ΔHEA, ΔHEA1, ΔHelectron affinity or ΔHfirst electron affinity. If symbols and words are given, I the symbols.
CON electron affinity of chloride / Cl– / Cl2

points.text: (enthalpy of) atomisation (of Cl) or bond energy (Cl–Cl) and (first) electron affinity (of chlorine)

explanation.text: Start from the element in its standard state, ½Cl2(g). Two steps take it to Cl–(g): first make one mole of gaseous chlorine atoms (enthalpy change of atomisation of chlorine, which is half the Cl–Cl bond energy), then add one electron to each atom (first electron affinity of chlorine). The sum of these two steps is the enthalpy change of formation of Cl–(g) defined in the question.

reasoningChain: Write the overall change: ½Cl₂(g) → Cl⁻(g).
Step 1: ½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g), atomisation (from the Cl–Cl bond energy).
Step 2: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g), first electron affinity of chlorine.

inferredMistakes.text: Naming the electron affinity of chloride, Cl⁻ or Cl₂, which the MS treats as a contradiction; the electron is added to a chlorine atom.
Giving ionisation energy, which removes an electron and is not needed to form an anion.

stem.text: The lattice energy of magnesium chloride, MgCl2, is –2493 kJ mol–1.
Use this value, and other data given, to calculate the enthalpy change of formation, in kJ mol–1, of MgCl2(s).

guidance: ecf use of 1x – 243 for ans = –400 (working needed).

explanation.text: Use the energy cycle: Mg(s) + Cl2(g) → Mg2+(g) + 2Cl–(g) → MgCl2(s). The first stage is the sum of the two ion formation values given in (d): +2336 for Mg2+(g) and 2 × (–243) for two moles of Cl–(g). The second stage is the lattice energy, –2493. So ΔHf = 2336 + 2(–243) + (–2493) = –643 kJ mol–1.

reasoningChain: Note the formula MgCl₂ needs two moles of Cl⁻(g): 2 × (–243) = –486.
Add the Mg²⁺(g) value: 2336 – 486 = +1850 kJ mol⁻¹.
Add the lattice energy: 1850 – 2493 = –643 kJ mol⁻¹.

inferredMistakes.text: Using the chloride ion value only once, giving –400 kJ mol⁻¹, which can only earn ecf credit when working is shown.
Subtracting the lattice energy instead of adding it, so its sign is reversed.

stem.text: Magnesium carbonate, MgCO<sub>3</sub>, decomposes when heated.

MgCO3 → MgO + CO2
ΔS = +175 J K–1 mol–1
ΔH = +117 kJ mol–1
Predict whether the decomposition of MgCO<sub>3</sub> is feasible at 600 °C.
Use a calculation to explain your answer.

guidance: CON G for ΔG but do not penalise twice If in words we need ‘change’.

points.text: M1 Correct ΔG = ΔH – TΔS and use of T = 873
M3 it is (feasible) and ΔG is negative / ΔG is less than zero UNC (Note: ΔG now in bold)

after: M3 is UNConditional on the basis it is a correct answer on the answer line. If the calculation has not been worked through to an answer, or has given a negative value for ΔG, there is no M3 for ‘not feasible because ΔG is positive’.

explanation.text: Use the Gibbs equation ΔG = ΔH – TΔS with consistent units and an absolute temperature. 600 °C = 873 K, and ΔS must be changed to kJ: +175 J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> = +0.175 kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>. Then ΔG = 117 – 873 × 0.175 = 117 – 152.8 = –35.8 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>. A negative ΔG means the reaction is feasible at this temperature.
The reaction is endothermic but has a positive entropy change, so the –TΔS term grows as the temperature rises. At 600 °C it is large enough to outweigh ΔH, so the sign of ΔG decides the prediction.

reasoningChain: Convert the temperature: 600 + 273 = 873 K.
Convert ΔS to kJ: 175 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 0.175 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Calculate ΔG = 117 – (873 × 0.175) = –35.8 kJ mol⁻¹.
ΔG is negative, so the decomposition is feasible at 600 °C.

inferredMistakes.text: Using T = 600 instead of 873 K, which gives ΔG = +12 kJ mol⁻¹ and earns only ecf credit.
Not converting ΔS from J to kJ, which gives a huge negative ΔG.
Writing G instead of ΔG, which the MS treats as a contradiction.

stem.text: Calcium carbonate, CaCO<sub>3</sub>, also decomposes when heated.
State whether the decomposition of CaCO<sub>3</sub> occurs at a higher or lower temperature than that of MgCO<sub>3</sub>. Explain your answer.

guidance: ⚫✓✓ any two for one mark. All three for two marks.
or group 2 trend but up / down the group must be clear.
or C-O / C=O bond (must be identified, e.g. C–O) is less weakened by Ca2+.

points.text: (In CaCO3) less distortion / polarisation of anion / COxy– ora

after: ora for MgCO3 but must be stated

explanation.text: Group 2 carbonates become more thermally stable down the group. The carbonate ion is large and easily distorted. A small 2+ cation such as Mg<sup>2+</sup> has a strong polarising effect: it pulls electron density towards itself and weakens the C–O bonds in the carbonate ion, so CO<sub>2</sub> is released more easily. Ca<sup>2+</sup> has the same charge but a larger ionic radius, so it polarises the carbonate ion less, and CaCO<sub>3</sub> needs a higher temperature to decompose.
The three points are marked separately: any two score [1] and all three score [2]. A comparison has to say clearly which ion is larger or which carbonate is distorted less.

reasoningChain: State the direction: CaCO₃ decomposes at a higher temperature.
Compare the cations: Ca²⁺ has a larger ionic radius than Mg²⁺ (same charge).
Link to the anion: Ca²⁺ polarises/distorts the carbonate ion less, so its C–O bonds are weakened less.

inferredMistakes.text: Explaining the trend by ionic bond or lattice strength, which the MS ignores.
Comparing atomic radius instead of ionic radius, which the MS ignores.
Saying Ca²⁺ is more polarising, which reverses the trend.

issues.note: 本题 (a)–(e) 共 12 分属于第 23 章（晶格能/Born–Haber 23.1，Gibbs 23.4），(f) 2 分属于 27.1（第 2 族碳酸盐热稳定性），所以 home 定为第 23 章跨章题。
MS guidance 原文印的是 "A attractive force × distance." / "A electrostatic attraction × distance."，PDF 文字层该字符是 Symbol 字体的 0xB4（乘号 ×）。从化学含义看更可能是想写 ∝ 1/distance 之类，疑似原文排版错误，照抄为 ×。
QP 的答题位置是三条横线，左下标 most negative、右下标 least negative，下面是 explanation 线。站内用一个 answerLines 块近似表示（"most negative ........ ........ ........ least negative" 和 "explanation"），不是逐字原文。
考纲没有"气态离子的生成焓"这一条；按 Born–Haber 循环的构建（23.1(3)）作 primary，23.1(1) 原子化焓、23.1(2) 第一电子亲和能作 secondary。
